sections.h: In Daniel 9: the prayer and its answer
sections.b: Chapter 9 gives the passage its setting. Daniel reads Jeremiah's seventy years (9:2), fasts and confesses (9:3-19), and Gabriel answers while Daniel is still praying (9:20-23). The six goals of 9:24 answer the confession. The passage's grammar leaves many choices open: the Hebrew has no verb between the numbers in 9:25, no named subject in 9:27, and a Ketiv/Qere in 9:24. Each is set out in the notes.

Gabriel interprets the ram and goat vision (8:16-26) and returns, 'whom I had seen in the vision at the start', to give the seventy sevens (9:21-27). The first angel named in the Bible, the meaning of his name is debated ('man of God' or 'God is my strength').

sections.h: Daniel 8-10: the ram and goat, the seventy sevens, the man in linen
sections.b: Chapter 8 (Hebrew again) pictures Persia as a two-horned ram and Greece as a goat, with a small horn from the goat's four horns whose rule over the temple lasts 2,300 evenings and mornings. Chapter 9 gives Daniel's prayer of confession and Gabriel's answer, the seventy sevens. Chapter 10, in the third year of Cyrus, gives a vision of a man in linen who describes a struggle with the princes of Persia and Greece.

Michael appears first as 'one of the chief princes' who helps the angel against 'the prince of the kingdom of Persia' (10:13), then as 'your prince' (10:21). The angel says that he alone stands firm with him against the princes of Persia and Greece. Michael is Israel's heavenly patron, as the 'prince of Persia' is Persia's (compare Deuteronomy 32:8-9).

Daniel 10 pictures angels set over nations: a 'prince of Persia', a 'prince of Greece', and Michael over Israel. The idea comes from Deuteronomy 32:8-9 in its Qumran and Greek reading ('the number of the sons of God'), and is stated in Sirach 17:17 and Jubilees 15:31-32. Rashi (read on Sefaria) says the prince of Persia asked God for a longer rule over Israel.

sections.h: The princes of Persia and Greece
sections.b: In Daniel 10, nations have heavenly 'princes' who struggle with the angel and with Michael. It is the clearest case in the Bible of the idea behind Deuteronomy 32:8-9 and Psalm 82: the gods of the nations are real powers under the Most High, limited and answerable to him.

sections.h: The rebellion that desolates and the abomination (Daniel 8:13; 9:27)
sections.b: The phrase first appears as 'the rebellion that desolates' (pesha shomem, 8:13); in 9:27 the Hebrew has 'on the wing of abominations one who makes desolate'. The wording seems to twist 'ba'al shamem', the Syrian name for Zeus Olympios, whose altar Antiochus IV set up in December 167 BC. In Daniel 9:27 it belongs to the last seven, and in the Greek the abomination stands 'on the temple'. The Greek rendering is what Matthew 24:15 and Mark 13:14 quote (see the note at Daniel 11:31).

Daniel 8:9-14, 23-25 describes a king from the Greek successor kingdoms who attacks the 'Beautiful Land', stops the regular offering and fights 'the prince of princes'; most scholars read Antiochus IV (175-164 BC).

Daniel 8 and 9 describe, in code, the attack on the temple (167 BC) that led to the revolt, in a vision of a horn that ends the regular offering, and in the 'covenant with the many' and 'abomination' of 9:27. The reading of these chapters as the Maccabean crisis dates back to Porphyry in the 3rd century AD.

The he-goat that crosses the earth without touching the ground (8:5) is the king of Greece (8:21), usually read as Alexander, whose conquest of Persia (334-331 BC) and early death (323 BC) are pictured by the breaking of the great horn and the four horns (8:8, 22).

In Daniel 8 Persia and Media are a two-horned ram (8:20). In 9:1 Darius the Mede reigns over the Chaldeans, and in 10:1 Cyrus of Persia is in his third year. In 10:13, 20 the 'prince of Persia' is the heavenly power set over the empire.

sections.h: Daniel's use of the seventy years (Daniel 9)
sections.b: In the first year of Darius, Daniel understands from the scrolls that the seventy years of Jeremiah are drawing to an end (9:2). His prayer is a response. Gabriel's answer turns the seventy years into seventy sevens (9:24), the earliest known reinterpretation of Jeremiah's prophecy, which the Qumran and later readers continued.

Daniel 9:25 speaks of 'an anointed one, a ruler' after seven sevens and 9:26 of an 'anointed one' who is cut off after sixty-two. The Hebrew has no article and no capital: the word is the ordinary 'anointed'. Cyrus, Jeshua, Zerubbabel, Onias III and Jesus have all been proposed. The Qumran Melchizedek scroll (11Q13) reads 'anointed prince' of an end-time figure.

sections.h: To anoint a most holy place (Daniel 9:24)
sections.b: The last of the six goals is 'to anoint a most holy place' (qodesh qodashim), which may be the temple's inner room or altar rededicated in 164 BC, a person (Jesus), a heavenly sanctuary, or a future temple.

Daniel's prayer is a model of confession: God is faithful and in the right, the people have sinned and rebelled, the curse of the law has fallen, and God is asked to act for his own name. It echoes Solomon's prayer (1 Kings 8:46-53), Ezra 9, Nehemiah 1 and 9, and Psalm 79. Baruch 1:15-3:8 reworks it.

Daniel prays 'with fasting, sackcloth and ashes' in 9:3 and in 10:2-3 mourns three weeks of days, eating no fine food, meat or wine and using no oil. The second is a partial fast; the angel says his words were heard from the first day (10:12).

The 'regular offering' (tamid) is the daily burnt offering of Exodus 29:38-42 and Numbers 28:3-8. The small horn takes it away (8:11); Antiochus' decree in 167 BC stopped it (1 Maccabees 1:45). The stopping of 'sacrifice and offering' in the middle of the last seven (9:27) is read of Antiochus, Christ's death, AD 70 or a future Antichrist.

The word nitsdaq in 8:14 is unique; Adventists tie it to the Day of Atonement's cleansing of the sanctuary and the 2,300 days to 1844. Others read the rededication of the temple in 164 BC, now kept at Hanukkah.

sections.h: The half of the seventieth seven (Daniel 9:27)
sections.b: 'In the middle of the seven' the sacrifice stops: half of seven is three and a half years, the length of 'a time, times and half a time' (7:25; 12:7). In the Maccabean reading this is 167-164 BC; in the messianic reading Jesus' ministry; in the dispensational reading the middle of the coming tribulation.

'The time of the end' (8:17, 19) and 'the last days' (10:14) introduce what the angel will tell. In the Antiochene reading the end is that of the persecution; in the futurist reading the end of the age.
